What is the most promising propulsion technology for theoretical manned Interstellar travel? What percentage of the speed of light could be theoretically reached? The question of interstellar travel is a fascinating one, riddled with both immense possibilities and seemingly insurmountable hurdles. The sheer distance between stars poses the most significant challenge, demanding incredibly efficient and powerful propulsion systems. But what does this even look like? There is a plethora of theoretical technologies bandied about, each with its own set of limitations. Fusion propulsion, perhaps, with its promise of harnessing the raw power of nuclear fusion, could offer the most promising avenue, potentially achieving a significant fraction of the speed of light. A “significant fraction” being the key phrase, and, as you might guess, a relative term. Depending on the specific design, and the availability of fuel, you could potentially reach 10% to maybe even 20% of lightspeed with a fusion-powered vessel.Next, Antimatter propulsion. This is a concept that, in theory, would give you a near-instant burst of energy from the complete annihilation of matter and antimatter. The concept is alluring, but also presents the obvious problem of producing, storing, and safely using antimatter. This is not easy, but one could imagine perhaps getting to, say 50% of the speed of light, or perhaps even significantly higher, dependent on the safety and supply factors.Then there is the ramjet. Interstellar objects such as gas clouds would serve as fuel and as such could allow for indefinite acceleration. The idea is to use the interstellar medium as a fuel source, scooping up hydrogen and using it for fusion reactions. Though, this idea carries with it its own set of constraints, one having to do with the density of the interstellar medium, and the resulting drag that would increase exponentially, as you get closer to lightspeed. It’s a long shot, and perhaps one that would only allow for a modest fraction of the speed of light.Finally, the Bussard ramjet, which is a theoretical concept that uses magnetic fields to collect interstellar hydrogen as fuel for a fusion reactor. This concept suggests that it could theoretically approach nearly the speed of light. All of this is theoretical, mind you, and the feasibility of each approach is currently limited by technological and engineering constraints. But, assuming we can overcome these issues, the dream of interstellar travel may one day become a reality.

I always read Victor Toth that the singularity is a moment in the future, not a point in place. What will happen to an observer falling into a black hole as he sees it for himself? Will he be crushed? The accepted wisdom is that an observer falling into a sufficiently large black hole wouldn’t experience a crushing end. The strong tidal forces near the event horizon would grow gradually, and the observer, if large enough, would feel a slight stretching in the radial direction and an equally slight compression in the orthogonal, tangential direction. Though still a highly unpleasant experience, the observer wouldn’t be torn apart until much closer to the singularity. This is not to say it would be a pleasant experience. The “tidal forces” I mentioned are gravitational forces that affect the observer due to the fact that the gravitational field in the vicinity of an object varies, depending on the observer's distance from the center and on the size of the object. The gradient of that field is strongest near the singularity, but the closer we approach the singularity, the faster the field increases. So, at some point, the gradient of the field becomes too strong, and the observer turns into spaghetti. The singularity, according to general relativity’s calculations, is the point where spacetime curves infinitely. Of course, general relativity’s predictions do not hold near the singularity because it does not take quantum-mechanical effects into account. We may need a theory of quantum gravity to really understand it, but we don’t have one! So the observer would not “see” anything after crossing the event horizon. The observer would, however, continue to exist, at least for a bit. He might reach the singularity. Or not. Either way, the observer has no information to communicate to the outside. What would an outside observer see? Well, that’s a whole other can of worms.

Why is it challenging to comprehend quantum mechanics? Can we simply accept Einstein's perspective on reality instead of the concept of uncertainty? The unsettling reality of quantum mechanics stems from its stark departure from our everyday experiences. We navigate a world governed by classical physics, a realm where objects possess definite properties and follow predictable trajectories. A tennis ball, for instance, has a precise location and momentum at any given moment, and we can, in principle, predict its future path with remarkable accuracy. Quantum mechanics, however, dismantles this intuitive picture. It introduces concepts like superposition and entanglement, where particles can exist in multiple states simultaneously and become intrinsically linked, regardless of distance. This inherent unpredictability challenges our classical understanding of cause and effect, making it difficult to reconcile with our ingrained sense of how the universe should function. Many, including the esteemed Albert Einstein, wrestled with the implications of quantum mechanics. Einstein, famously, found the probabilistic nature of quantum mechanics deeply unsettling, famously quipping that he didn't believe "God plays dice with the world". The concept of objective reality, where properties are definitively possessed, was something Einstein clung to. He steadfastly argued for a more complete theory, one that would restore determinism, a theory that, so far, has not been found.

Can antimatter be considered as "visible matter" because it can interact with light even though it has the opposite charge of normal matter? The term "visible matter" is a misnomer, and here's why. It’s tempting to assume that anything that interacts with light falls under this category. However, the descriptor "visible" has a very specific meaning, confined to the range of wavelengths our eyes can perceive. Think of it less as a universal label and more as a subjective characteristic, determined by the limitations of our own biological detectors. To put it differently, "visible" refers to stuff that reflects or emits light within the narrow band of the electromagnetic spectrum that stimulates the photoreceptors in our retinas. Antimatter, in principle, shares this ability. When it interacts with its matter counterpart, the annihilation event produces photons, ergo, light. The crucial question is, what type of light? The energy involved, determining the frequency, dictates the story. In fact, it does not have to involve “visible light." The annihilation process invariably produces high-energy photons (gamma rays), completely outside the visible spectrum, which is to say, we can't see it, and, in many cases, deadly if you're close enough. So, if we were to witness an electron and a positron annihilate, we wouldn’t see a flash of light, per se, but a burst of energetic radiation, detectable using very different devices. Ultimately, it comes down to the method of detection. While antimatter certainly interacts with photons, does it qualify as "visible"? The answer is nuanced, as always.

If a human somehow managed to travel to the Sagittarius A* black hole, would they see exactly what the 2022 image shows us? No, the human wouldn’t see precisely that, for a plethora of reasons. The image, after all, is a reconstruction, a result of painstaking efforts, from data collected by the Event Horizon Telescope. Moreover, the EHT itself is not a single, giant telescope, but rather a network of radio telescopes scattered across the globe, all working in concert. Crucially, the human observer is not a radio telescope, and the human’s brain is not a supercomputer that can process terabytes of data and use sophisticated algorithms that account for things like the Earth’s rotation, atmospheric effects, and the interstellar medium—all of which can, and do, smear, distort, and otherwise obscure the incredibly faint signal emanating from the vicinity of the supermassive black hole. Even if the human had access to the raw data, the human’s eyes are not sensitive to radio waves; the telescope captures them just fine, but human sight cannot. Then there’s the issue of timescale: even if the human could somehow magically see radio waves with their eyes, the image is not a real-time direct view as the image of Sagittarius A* is produced over all the observations the network has made. The real-time evolution of the accretion disk, gas swirling in the black hole, and particle jets is not something the image captures. Further, even if the observer were to equip themselves with the finest radio telescope in the world, there are more problems: the human would be exposed to extreme gravitational and magnetic fields. Approaching the black hole would be an exercise in self-destruction on any practical timescale. The strong tidal forces, the spaghettification, would begin to take effect long before the observer had a chance to see anything. And one more thing: even if our hypothetical human somehow survived the trip and possessed the ability to “see” what the telescope sees, there would be a certain angle that the black hole’s gravity would bend light. This would be the angle of deflection. But no matter how great one’s capacity for observation, it would be virtually impossible to see the sort of ring that the EHT captured.

Dear Viktor Toth, with respect to your answer on the expression of the weak force, could you please correct the second equation? The first one for V(r) is right, but the second seems to have a typo, so that it is not displayed. Indeed, you are right. My apologies. The second equation was garbled. Let me provide a suitable correction, and a bit of context. When we speak of the weak force, we are primarily interested in how it is mediated by the W and Z bosons, which, in turn, are responsible for radioactive decay. We are usually concerned with the potential energy *V(r)* between two particles separated by a distance *r*. The first equation describes the effective electrostatic potential *V(r)* between two charged particles, which is given via *V(r) = q1q2/4πε₀r *, where *q1* and *q2* are their respective charges, and where as usual, *ε₀* is the electric constant, the permittivity of free space. The equivalent formula for the weak force is a bit more complicated because the force carriers, the W and Z bosons, are massive particles. So instead of the familiar Coulomb potential, we have a Yukawa potential, which is given by *V(r) = g1g2exp(-µr)/4πεr*. Here, *g1* and *g2* are the weak charges of the two particles, *µ* is the mass of the force carrier multiplied by the speed of light, and *ħ=h/2π* where *h* is Planck’s constant. It must be emphasized here that unlike photons, the W and Z bosons have significant mass, which is why quantum field theory works the way that it does. A rather counter-intuitive aspect of all of this is that unlike electromagnetism, the weak force is not, in and of itself, responsible for the binding of matter. It only appears, in a rather complicated fashion, when we solve the more interesting cases, such as beta decay. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

How is the speed of light considered constant in all frames despite the effects of gravitational and inertial time dilation? That's a perceptive question, and the answer gets to the heart of how Einstein's theory of relativity works. It's a matter of careful definitions, and of appreciating the inherent complexities of spacetime. First, let's remember the basics: the speed of light in a vacuum, often denoted as *c* (approximately 299,792,458 meters per second), is a fundamental constant. It's a universal speed limit, and, crucially, it's a constant *in all inertial frames of reference*. This is one of the two foundational postulates of special relativity. But “inertial frames” are the key word here; they are those not accelerating. Gravitational and inertial time dilation are both predictions of general relativity, which deals with accelerating frames, hence special relativity doesn't apply. Time dilation, whether due to gravity or acceleration—and remember, from the equivalence principle, the two cannot be told apart—is not a “distortion” of the speed of light itself. Instead, it's a distortion of spacetime, and of the observer's experience of time relative to someone in a "still" (or more correctly, a non-accelerating) frame of reference. Imagine two observers, Alice and Bob. Alice is in a strong gravitational field, near a massive object, while Bob is far away from any significant gravitational influence. Alice experiences time more slowly than Bob. From Bob's perspective, light emitted by Alice will appear to travel slower, because Alice's "tick" has slowed, meaning that her 'second' is slower. From Alice’s perspective however, light goes at its typical constant speed. This is how light moves at its constant speed in all frames of reference: It is affected by a complex process where the passage of time is warped. It is not changing light's speed. So, when the light then reaches Bob the light will appear to reach Bob at the time he measures to be further in the future. This shows that spacetime is not a simple Euclidean space with a separate and independent dimension of time. It is a unified fabric where space and time are intertwined, and gravity warps that fabric, which then changes the measurements of space and time and therefore the light. What are tensors (as used in special/general relativity) exactly? Tensors, in the context of relativity, are best understood as mathematical objects that transform in a specific way under a change of coordinates. Think of them as generalizations of scalars (quantities with no direction, like temperature) and vectors (quantities with both magnitude and direction), and they don't depend on your choice of coordinate system. The key is this transformation rule. When you switch coordinate systems (imagine, say, describing a point using Cartesian coordinates versus polar coordinates), a tensor's components will change, but the tensor itself, the underlying geometrical object it represents, stays the same. It's similar to how the length of a vector remains constant regardless of how you choose to describe it. A tensor is a multidimensional array (a matrix of matrices, etc.) with a specific number of indices. The number of indices determines its "rank" or "order". A scalar is a rank-0 tensor, a vector is a rank-1 tensor, a matrix is a rank-2 tensor, and so on. Each index represents a particular dimension or direction in space-time, and the values that the tensor takes at those indices, its "components", define the tensor's properties. These components transform according to a precise mathematical rule that ensures that the tensor's mathematical description remains physically consistent across all coordinate systems. This transformation rule is what makes tensors so useful in relativity, as it allows us to express physical laws in a coordinate-independent way. By utilizing tensors, we can formulate equations that describe how the universe works; these equations will always be valid, regardless of the observer's perspective or the chosen coordinate system.

Can a black hole at its center be destroyed? If so, what would be the method to do so? Would the intense gravity make it impossible to escape and cause any damage? Sadly, I can't give you a definite answer. The singularity at the heart of a black hole, the point where all the matter gets compressed, is still one of physics' biggest mysteries. We simply have no established theory to deal with it; general relativity tells us that its existence seems inevitable if enough matter condenses in a small enough volume, but it also breaks down when you try to describe it. Quantum mechanics offers some clues — the idea of spacetime itself being quantized, for instance — but a full-blown theory of quantum gravity, which could possibly describe the singularity, is still beyond us. So, can a singularity in a black hole be destroyed? In principle, yes. The energy density is infinite; there’s literally nothing left. The problem with a black hole, however, is information: as far as we know today, and unless quantum gravity eventually tells us otherwise, all the information about what went into a black hole is lost once it crosses the event horizon. With no information, this would simply mean the singularity has existed since it was formed, and has never been destroyed. As for the "how,” this is where things become even more complicated. The intense gravity is what keeps everything inside, preventing anything, even light, from escaping. If you tried to "destroy" the central singularity, assuming that this is even theoretically possible, by, say, feeding another singularity to it, gravity would still be the primary player in this event, causing any conceivable damage. It seems rather likely that the process would simply result in a larger, more massive black hole. As for escaping, that, too, is impossible. But as I said, this is all theoretical speculation, and unfortunately, we don't have the scientific tools just yet to make any definitive statement about singularities within black holes. What is the definition of observation in the double-slit interference experiment of light? Can the visual observation of intelligent creatures determine whether light is a particle or a wave? The short answer to your question is that “observation” in the double-slit experiment has nothing to do with human perception or the act of looking, but rather with any interaction that reveals “which way” the particle went. To flesh that out, let us start with the basics: according to quantum mechanics, light (and indeed, everything else) behaves both as a wave and a particle. A wave is a disturbance that propagates in a medium, whereas a particle is a discrete, localized entity. When light travels from a source to a detector, it behaves as a wave, spreading out and interfering with itself, which is why we see an interference pattern. When the light is detected, however, it behaves as a particle, with its energy concentrated in a specific location. In the double-slit experiment, this wave-particle duality is revealed when light passes through two slits. If no attempt is made to determine which slit the light particle goes through, the light exhibits wave-like behavior, creating an interference pattern on a distant screen. But, if we try to “observe” which slit the light particle goes through, the interference pattern disappears, and the light behaves as a particle, creating two distinct bands on the screen. This is one of the most fundamental, most mind-bending experiments in all of modern physics, a cornerstone of the Copenhagen interpretation of quantum mechanics. The measurement itself, not the act of looking at the experiment, is what causes the change in behavior. The “observation” can be performed by any device or interaction that reveals which slit the light particle went through, whether it be a photon detector, a magnetic field, or even a clever arrangement of mirrors. It is the interaction that changes the wave-like behavior to particle-like behavior. The role of an intelligent creature is irrelevant. Observing, in the quantum mechanical sense, means measuring the position and/or momentum of a particle. The observer is, literally, the measuring apparatus.

Is it a coincidence that all particles with Higgs mass carry electric charges? That is a very good question, and the answer is, somewhat surprisingly, “yes”. At least, in the Standard Model of particle physics, the observed fact that all particles acquire their mass from the Higgs field and also carry electric charge is purely coincidental! Actually, the Higgs field's coupling to charged particles is not a coincidence, but the relation between electric charge and mass is: you can have one without the other. The Higgs field couples to fermions via their “Yukawa interactions.” These interactions involve the Higgs field and also gauge fields which are, in turn, responsible for the transfer of fundamental forces. It turns out that these Yukawa interactions are what give massive fermions their mass through what is known as “spontaneous symmetry breaking.” However, there is no fundamental reason why these Yukawa interactions, and therefore the mass of elementary particles, should be correlated with the charges of these particles. You could easily construct a model where the Higgs field interacts with a particle to give it mass but does not affect its charge, or vice versa. This is just the way things happen to work out in our universe, at least in the Standard Model. And even if the universe were different, that fact would not fundamentally change the explanation. The Higgs field is not responsible for electric charge. The particles’ charges are determined by the other interactions in the Standard Model, namely, the electromagnetic interaction mediated by the photon. The way the Higgs field couples the fermions, has nothing to do with their electric charges. In principle, other interactions, such as those mediated by the W and Z bosons, also contribute to mass. But the Higgs field is by far the dominant contributor for all fermions, and all particles other than the photon and the gluons. And as a matter of fact, the electromagnetic and the weak interactions are unified into one single interaction, called the electroweak interaction, so the Higgs interactions are, in the end, intertwined with the electromagnetic interaction. It is just that in order for them to co-exist, all particles which interact with the Higgs field need to carry electric charges. However, there is no underlying law to mandate this. It is just the specifics of how things are constructed that require it. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Why are the negative energy solutions to Dirac equation interpreted as antimatters instead of virtual matters? The simplest answer lies in recognizing the meaning of a quantum-mechanical wave function. In the Dirac equation, the wave function describes the probability amplitude of finding certain properties, such as position and momentum, for a particle. The negative-energy solutions, in and of themselves, are not something that can be directly observed. They don't represent a "virtual matter" state that can be realized with observation. If we consider the Dirac equation in its complete form, the negative-energy solutions are a mathematical necessity; you cannot simply eliminate them and maintain the self-consistency of the equations. Historically, the interpretation of negative-energy solutions stemmed from several conceptual confusions surrounding the idea of negative energy. It’s important to remember that the energy of a particle can certainly be negative, relative to some reference point or potential well. But the interpretation of negative energy solutions, as they appear in the Dirac equation, are not meant to be taken literally. They do not describe physical objects that are in a perpetual state of negative energy. To understand the negative-energy solutions, we must consider the context of quantum field theory (QFT) and, specifically, Dirac’s “hole theory.” In modern QFT, we interpret the negative-energy solutions as representing anti-particles. They represent a state of positive energy, but with opposite charges and other quantum numbers of the original particle. Think of it like this: a negative-energy electron is equivalent to a positive-energy, positively charged anti-electron, which we call a positron. This is not a perfect analogy, mind you, because Dirac’s original thinking on the matter predated the development of modern “quantum field theory” and concepts like “particle-antiparticle duality.” This interpretation provides a conceptual bridge from the mathematical to the physical. But the essence of it is that negative energy solutions are not directly observable, but they are indicative of the existence of anti-particles. In 3 dimensions, Cartesian coordinate systems are distinguishable from their mirror images. What is the situation in 3+1 dimensions and how many inequivalent images are there? Given its four-dimensional nature, it's a trickier question than just flipping a hand, or a coordinate axis, as we're accustomed to in everyday, three-dimensional space. In 3+1 dimensions, this concept becomes more intricate. When we look at a spacetime coordinate system, a “mirror image” isn't quite as straightforward; there is no intuitive concept we can grasp here. The mathematical description is one of the key features in the study of parity transformations, a kind of reflection that reverses a spatial axis. In physics, we ask about the behavior of a physical system under such transformations. This is because the basic equations of physics may, or may not, behave in the same way under a parity transformation. An example of this is the weak interaction, which violates parity. One of the defining characteristics of our universe is that it behaves differently under the action of parity transformations. It is not reflection symmetric. Now back to the question. The number of inequivalent images in a 3+1 system can be derived from the properties of spacetime: one time dimension, three space dimensions, plus something called the metric tensor, which encodes the geometry of spacetime and the behavior of light in it. In standard special and general relativity, the metric tensor has a specific form, dictating how we measure lengths and times. Its properties limit the possible coordinate transformations and constrain the number of inequivalent images. Unlike the 3-dimensional case where you just have two types, “right-handed” and “left-handed,” in 3+1 dimensions, the situation is again more complicated. To keep things simple, we do have one extra factor: time. Reversing the time coordinate can also be a relevant transformation in a physical theory. Usually the systems of interest have some kind of symmetry properties, meaning physical laws stay the same when we reflect, or rotate. But we still have the option of considering parity transformations that involve spatial coordinate inversions. To be precise, the answer relies on the details of how each coordinate axis is defined relative to others. One way is to classify coordinate systems based on their orientation. Without the complete set of equations, describing how the axes are aligned, the number of such inequivalent images, in practice, depends on the context.

When the particle is being observed, does its wave function collapse into a size less point, or a very small Gaussian packet? The key here is the word “collapse”. It is the term and the concept everyone loves to hate. The textbook explanation typically goes something like this: you start with a wave function that describes all the possible positions of the particle in the universe. And then, when you observe it (by, say, measuring its position or momentum), the wave function suddenly “collapses” into a single point at the place where you found the particle (the Copenhagen interpretation). Or, at the very least, its wave function “collapses” into a very small Gaussian packet around the measured value (the many-worlds interpretation). But what does all this really mean in terms of the equations? Do we modify the wave function at the instant of the observation? Or is the evolution of the wave function continuous until we make a measurement, at which point we just see the result? Well, it depends. But one thing is certain: the concept of wave function “collapse” is very vague. And it has been a source of confusion for physicists for almost a century. In fact, it is a common misconception that we can describe a particle’s position as a single point. The reality, per quantum mechanics, is far more nuanced. We have to first define what it means to “observe” a particle, then consider the various interpretations, and finally, try to reconcile the math with the physical reality. And don’t get me started on the role of the observer. A simple measurement could be as complex as a collision of two photons or as mundane as the interaction with a detector. Which of those requires a “collapse”? I’ll leave that as an exercise to the reader. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Is a single electron considered an actual particle in quantum mechanics, or is it always just a wave packet with definite properties at any given time? Ah, the age-old question! Is the electron a point-like particle, a fuzzy cloud of probability, or something in between? The answer, as with so many things in the quantum realm, is a resounding “it depends.” The problem boils down to our persistent, classical biases. We want things to be either one or the other. A particle, we imagine, has a definite location, a defined trajectory. A wave, on the other hand, is spread out, a disturbance propagating through space. Quantum mechanics, however, tells us that the electron can behave as both, depending on how you look at it, or rather, how you measure it. When we perform a measurement, we “force” the electron to choose. If we try to pinpoint its location, we’ll find it at a specific spot, behaving like a particle. But in the process, we lose information about its momentum. Conversely, if we measure its momentum, we’ll find it spread out, with its position becoming less defined. The famous “wave packet” is a mathematical construct we use to describe this duality. It’s a superposition of different waves, each with a different momentum and wavelength, that, when combined, give us a probability distribution. It tells us where we are most likely to find the electron. But again, it's not as if the electron *is* the wave packet. It’s more like the wave packet *describes* our knowledge of the electron. The electron itself is still “itself,” whatever that is. In a double-slit experiment, for example, electrons go through both slits simultaneously (somehow!), creating an interference pattern, just like waves. In this case, the wave-like behavior prevails. Does any of this make sense? Probably not in a classically intuitive way. But therein lies the beauty, and the challenge, of quantum mechanics.

Does quantum mechanics contradict determinism? That's quite a loaded question, isn't it? The short answer is, well, it depends. And as with many of my forays into the realm of physics, the deeper you delve, the more complicated the answer becomes. Let's start with the basics. Classical physics, the physics we all intuitively understand, is deterministic. Given the initial conditions of a system, you can, in principle, predict its future behavior with absolute certainty. Think about a billiard ball. If you know its initial position, velocity, and the forces acting upon it (friction, the impact of other balls, etc.), you can calculate where it will be at any future time. Quantum mechanics, however, throws a wrench into this neat, predictable world. At its core, quantum mechanics is probabilistic. You *cannot* predict the future with certainty. Instead, you can only calculate the probabilities of different outcomes. Think about a radioactive atom. You can’t say precisely when it will decay, only the probability of it decaying within a given time frame. This inherent uncertainty is often seen as a challenge to determinism. If the universe is governed by probabilities, how can it be deterministic? It’s a good question and has spawned countless philosophical debates over the decades. One of the key tenets that often gets brought up is related to the interpretation of quantum mechanics. The Copenhagen interpretation, for example, views the act of measurement as fundamentally altering the system, collapsing the wave function and forcing a definite outcome. This suggests that the universe is not entirely deterministic, as the outcome of an event is determined by the act of observation itself. More recent interpretations, like the many-worlds interpretation, propose a different view. In this scenario, the wave function never collapses. Instead, every possible outcome of a quantum measurement is realized, each in its own separate 'world.' This interpretation tries to preserve determinism (albeit in a very bizarre way): the future is pre-determined, but it branches into an infinite number of possibilities. So, does quantum mechanics contradict determinism? It really hinges on which interpretation of quantum mechanics you subscribe to. Some interpretations explicitly reject determinism, embedding randomness or indeterminacy, while others, like many-worlds, attempt to salvage it albeit with a profound cost to our common-sense view of reality. It’s a fascinating puzzle, and one that physicists and philosophers continue to grapple with today. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Does Victor Toth agree that his explanation of the cosmic microwave background with the help of pops on the square is more suitable for "substantiating" the Olbers paradox? I am afraid that I do not have a clear memory of specific public positions taken by Victor Toth on this topic. However, I would like to point out an interesting point that is relevant nonetheless. If we consider the idea that the cosmic microwave background (CMB) offers a suitable argument against Olbers' paradox, we must take into account the fact that the CMB, as observed today, is quite uniform, suggesting a homogeneous universe on a very large scale. In other words, it suggests that sources of radiation were distributed fairly evenly throughout the early universe.This, of course, poses a problem. If the universe is infinitely old and infinite in extent, shouldn't every point in the sky be constantly bombarded with light from countless stars, making the night sky as bright as the surface of a star? This is the core of Olbers' paradox. If the CMB, which originates from a very early era, is uniform, then the observed uniformity itself could be considered an argument that refutes the assumptions of Olbers' paradox. Specifically, the universe, or at least the observable part of it, was not always transparent, and was not always populated with a constant density of stars. Instead, the universe had a beginning and has expanded to make distant objects appear red-shifted to the point where much of their light is not visible anymore. Therefore, the observed uniformity of CMB, which indicates a uniform distribution of sources in the early universe, may be, in some sense, an additional argument against the core assumptions of Olbers' paradox, even if not directly “substantiating” it in the way one could assume. Is MOND a statistical artifact and how do new gravity models answer the question of dark matter any more accurately? MOND, or Modified Newtonian Dynamics, is a proposed modification to Newton’s laws of gravity, and it's a fascinating area of astrophysical inquiry. The central idea behind MOND is to adjust our understanding of gravity at very low accelerations, a realm where we observe discrepancies in the rotation curves of galaxies, which is normally a key indicator of Dark Matter presence. It's a theoretical exploration, and as such, the question of whether it's a mere statistical artifact is a pertinent one. The crux of the matter, as far as how successfully MOND, or indeed any alternative gravity model deals with the Dark Matter issue, lies in accurately describing the observed behavior of galaxies and galaxy clusters, not just their rotation curves. The primary challenge lies in consistently explaining a broad range of astronomical observations without necessarily invoking a yet-unseen form of matter. Many models, some based on f(R) gravity, others incorporating scalar fields, offer various competing explanations. Yet, the effectiveness of any new gravity model in accounting for Dark Matter is a complex question. The answer rests on its predictive power beyond the basics. Does the model produce a viable description of phenomena such as gravitational lensing, the cosmic microwave background, and the large-scale structure of the universe? Does it account for the distribution of galaxies within a cluster? How it performs concerning the bullet cluster, where the gravitational lensing signal and the observed distribution of the visible matter are offset: a key indicator of problems with the model if it can't accurately portray how the matter is distributed in the cluster. In essence, while MOND and its successors may offer alternative explanations, they're assessed much like standard models, through their ability to predict and explain a wide range of cosmic data. What would it look like to see a planet go through a wormhole as an observer? It's a tough question, as we do not really know. I will venture to say, that we can try to imagine it. The simplest answer is to say that from an observer's perspective, it would look like a planet disappearing and reappearing at another place. But that explanation is a cop-out. The reason is that general relativity forbids “shortcuts” that may allow the planet to move faster than the speed of light. This is why wormholes are still in the realm of science fiction, as no one has figured out how to make one. In its basic form, a wormhole connects two distinct points in spacetime. The catch? You'd be traveling faster than the light, but everything you knew would be gone.

What is m in f=ma, rest mass, inertial mass, variable mass, or gravitational mass? When we write f=ma, m is the inertial mass. But beware, the equation can be misleading. The formula itself has no reference to gravity. If the force in question is gravity itself then, in the framework of Newtonian theory, the same m is acting in both cases: the inertial mass, which expresses inertia – resistance to a change of motion – and as the gravitational mass that mediates the interaction with gravity. But this is not always the case. For example, in special relativity, a non-zero velocity is assigned a non-zero momentum, and a force must be applied to accelerate a massive object. Here, inertial mass is identified with the object's resistance to acceleration but not with its gravitational behavior. If the m in f=ma were the same as that in F=GMm/r^2, the implication would be that if two objects of identical mass, at the same distance from a massive object, experience the same gravitational force, they would also respond to the same acceleration. This, however, is not always true. In general relativity, it turns out that it is not that force that matters, but the curvature of spacetime that dictates the acceleration, and that depends solely on the distribution of energy and momentum, not mass alone. So, which m in f=ma? It depends on the context. It has to be understood from the specific problem that we solve. The rest mass is an inherent property of a massive object.

Why a free isolated electon cant fully absorb a photon? Because energy and momentum must be conserved. And this is where it gets tricky, just as it does when we try to describe what happens when an electron and a positron annihilate (I just wrote about it, so I am familiar with the topic). The photon has energy E and momentum p = E/c. The electron has rest mass m and we can safely assume it is (initially) at rest in the reference frame of the observer, so its energy is E = mc 2 and momentum is zero. If the electron fully absorbed the photon, then, after the absorption, we would have new particle (the electron) with total energy 2mc² (or, equivalently, E = 2E electron ) and a momentum equal to E/c. But now, using the m 2 = ( E / c 2 ) 2 − ( p / c ) 2 relationship, we can see that that is not possible: after the absorption, the mass squared of the electron would have to be (2m)² - (E/c)² which is significantly different than the rest mass of a free electron. Since the final product of our experiment has to be the same object — an electron — no full absorption can happen. Now, if instead of an "isolated" electron, we were dealing with an electron bound to a nucleus, then the whole game changes. In that case, the nucleus will also be around. This nucleus carries a big mass, so a photon might well be absorbed, but the result will be a new electron state and the recoil of the whole atom. The atom is so much heavier than the electron, that the momentum of the absorbed photon can be compensated by the momentum of the atom with only a negligibly small exchange of energy. That’s what is known as a transition between “atomic levels”. The photon is absorbed, and the result is an excited (more energetic) state of the atom, and the change of momentum is effectively transferred to the atom as a whole. **Question for a physicist: ** How are stars born according to the general theory of relativity? General relativity, as I understand it, doesn't directly concern itself with the *birth* of stars per se, but rather the conditions under which they can exist and evolve. Essentially, it provides the framework for understanding the gravitational forces that govern the entire process. Stars are, at their core, born from the gravitational collapse of enormous clouds of gas and dust—primarily hydrogen and helium—known as nebulae. The general theory of relativity enters the picture, primarily via its description of how gravity works. As the nebula collapses which can be initiated by a number of events, such as a supernova blast from a nearby star or the spiral arms of a galaxy compressing the gas, gravity plays a crucial role. Once the cloud becomes dense enough, gravity overcomes the internal pressure of the gas, and the cloud collapses even further. The increasing compression leads to a rise in temperature. The core of the cloud becomes incredibly dense, and the internal heat is massive, but, more importantly, the core of the cloud is an increasingly massive gravitational ‘sink’. This gravitational effect is what defines what will happen at the core–the only escape is fusion! When the core temperature reaches a staggering 10 million degrees Celsius, the process of nuclear fusion ignites. At this point, the intense pressure and temperature within the core force hydrogen atoms to fuse, creating helium and releasing a tremendous amount of energy. This release counteracts the gravitational collapse, creating a state of equilibrium. This is the moment that a star is officially considered to be "born". General relativity does not provide any specific prediction how the star will appear, or whether or how soon, or under what conditions. But general relativity does explain what gravity is in this state. It dictates the behavior of space-time, it dictates how gravity warps space around a massive body. And so it shapes the very conditions in which stars can live, evolve, and eventually die.

Is it fair to say that there is the equivalent of infinite acceleration at the event horizon of a black hole? Not really. The question is a bit tricky, hinging on what one means by “equivalent”. The gravitational acceleration, or more descriptively, the tidal forces, felt by an object at the event horizon of a black hole are quite high. They're not infinite, of course. Even at the singularity (the actual center of a black hole, where all the mass is concentrated), where both general relativity and our intuition break down, you won't find an infinite value for anything. But the value is high, and it’s a strong function of the size of the black hole: the smaller the black hole, the larger the tidal forces at the event horizon. So, for a stellar mass black hole (say, three times the mass of the Sun), the tidal forces at the event horizon would be so immense that they would rip apart any object—including an unlucky astronaut. The force would be even stronger at the singularity, though, again, we would not be able to make a measurement of it. But as we get more massive black holes? Things change. For a supermassive black hole (like the one at the center of our galaxy, at roughly four million solar masses), the tidal forces are much less severe. So an astronaut could, in principle, cross the event horizon without experiencing any extreme effects. The reason is that the curvature of spacetime is less pronounced in supermassive black holes than in stellar ones. The force is still high, of course, but not as overwhelming as in the case of the smaller variety. It's like walking on a basketball versus walking on a bowling ball: the curvature is less pronounced on a larger sphere. So, no, it is not fair to say that you would feel infinite acceleration, but it is fair to say that the tidal forces at the event horizon of a small black hole are very strong (though still finite). But the true beauty of it: the smaller the black hole, the faster it evaporates, so if we are to witness the event, the universe will not wait for us. If all of the mass energy of colliding black holes is contained within their event horizons, how does the collision release any energy? Stuff can escape from the event horizon if it collides with another? That's the crux of the matter, isn't it? The very essence of a black hole, its defining characteristic, is that nothing, not even a photon, can escape its gravitational clutches once it crosses that event horizon. So, how can a collision, an event firmly within the boundaries of these cosmic behemoths, liberate energy? The answer lies in the intricate dance of spacetime itself. When black holes collide, they don't simply merge into a larger, static entity. Oh no, the universe puts on a show! The initial impact generates a violent distortion of spacetime, an immense wave that ripples outwards. This is where the energy escape is happening: these distortions, these gravitational waves, are not bound by the event horizon. They are the messengers, the outward expression of the cataclysmic event within, carrying away the liberated energy. Think of it like throwing a pebble into a pond: the water, analogous to spacetime, is disturbed, and waves radiate outwards, carrying the energy of the pebble's impact. In the case of colliding black holes, the "pebble" is the collision itself, and the "water" is the fabric of spacetime. These gravitational waves are the key; they are the energy that is *allowed* to escape, the only avenue of escape for the energy initially present within the black holes, locked away behind their respective event horizons. Granted, the details are immensely more complex, requiring General Relativity and advanced mathematics to fully describe, but the general concept is simple: spacetime itself is the medium through which the energy is released.

How do quarks give rise to the mass of protons and neutrons? This is a question with subtleties that often get lost in oversimplified explanations, and it’s best to start with a clarification: quarks give *most* of the mass. The mass of the proton and the neutron is surprisingly large compared to the sum of the masses of their constituent quarks. For instance, when we consider the “up” and “down” quarks that make up a proton and a neutron, their combined mass is a mere 1% of the mass of the proton and neutron. So, what comprises the remaining 99%? It's a complex interplay of factors. The majority arises from the energy of the gluons, the force-carrying particles that mediate the strong force, which binds quarks together. These gluons don’t have rest mass in the traditional sense, but they do possess energy, and thanks to Einstein’s famous equation (E=mc²), energy is directly proportional to mass. Then, there's the kinetic energy of the quarks themselves — their constant motion within the confines of the proton and neutron contributes to the overall mass. And finally, we can't overlook the mass contribution inherent in the strong interaction itself, like the "binding energy" of a bound state. All of these contributions combined – the kinetic energy of the quarks, the energy of the gluons, and the energy of their interactions – account for the dominant portion of the mass of a proton or a neutron.

A system composed by a piece of iron and a magnet has more energy if the iron is closer the magnet. So, the overall weight should be (very very slightly) different. Is there an intuitive thought experiment to show it? Well, yes, and it's a classic: the thought experiment by Einstein. Suppose you've got a box, a perfectly insulated box, containing at one end an emission source and at the other end a detector. You can imagine, for instance, that the emission source spews light. Thus the box, at any given time, has some amount of light energy bouncing back and forth within its walls. The detector can absorb the very same light: When that happens, the light energy is converted by the detector into its equivalent mass. What happens when the light leaves the source? The box will lose a teeny-tiny amount of mass. It's not that you created a box of nothing, of course: You still have light bouncing around inside the box; you still have the energy of the light. And that box still has all its mass, which is the same as before. Now, suppose we can move our emission source to the other side of the box. As the light travels, the box has the same net weight, and when the light is absorbed, the box's mass is changed in exactly the same way it was before. The box's contents (the light) are converted by the detector into its corresponding mass. It is what we mean when we say E = mc²: the energy of anything (be it the light of our thought experiment, the mass of the iron, or the magnetic properties of the magnet) and its rest mass is equivalent. So, yes, the overall weight of the system composed of the iron and the magnet should be (very, very slightly) different. And that's it, in a nutshell: The iron, when it’s closer to the magnet, is in a lower energy state, with less potential energy; the system weight should be slightly less.

Brian Greene said: “as particles … try to move through space, they have to burrow through the Higgs field, and that is what gives them mass”. Does that mean that particles that keep at rest in the frame of the Higgs fied are gravitationally massless? This is a rather clever reformulation of a seemingly innocuous and oft-repeated talking point: the Higgs field’s role in bestowing mass on fundamental particles. My knee-jerk reaction is, as usual, to become a pedant, but this strikes me as a genuinely interesting query that warrants thoughtful consideration. Indeed, if a particle were to remain perfectly stationary relative to the Higgs field – a scenario difficult to conceive, given our understanding of the universe, but let us entertain it for the sake of argument – would it be impervious to the gravitational pull of other massive bodies? The answer hinges on a subtle but crucial distinction between inertial and gravitational mass, a distinction that, regrettably, is often blurred in popular science discussions. The “mass” that the Higgs field is concerned with is the inertial mass. This mass is the measure of an object's resistance to acceleration, its reluctance to change its state of motion. Essentially, it is the quantity that appears in Newton’s second law of motion: F = ma. On the other hand, the “mass” that governs gravity – the mass that determines the strength of the gravitational force between two objects – is the gravitational mass. Now, it is extremely well-established through experiments that these two masses are, at least to a very high degree of precision, equivalent. This is the bedrock of Einstein's principle of equivalence. Therefore, if a particle "acquires" inertial mass from its interaction with the Higgs field, that same mass also dictates how strongly it interacts with the gravitational field. So, back to the hypothetical particle, even if glued rigidly to the Higgs, it would still possess gravitational mass and experience gravity in the regular fashion. However, I must add some reservations. This is a very high level description and I might have missed something.

How does a black hole destroy matter but not light? Light is a massless particle. As such, its interaction with spacetime (i.e., gravity) is profoundly different from that of anything with a mass. The key is that a black hole isn't really "destroying" anything. What a black hole does is to distort the spacetime geometry around it to such an extreme extent that it is virtually impossible for anything, including light, to escape, provided that they get too close. A black hole is defined by its event horizon: a boundary beyond which nothing, not even light, can escape. So, to explain it simply: anything that falls inside the black hole's event horizon is effectively "gone" from the outside universe. However, while light cannot "escape" a black hole, light can and will still interact with the gravitational field of the black hole, and it will interact in a very peculiar way. It will be bent (gravitationally lensed) and its frequency will be "redshifted" (i.e., as the light travels towards the black hole, it increasingly loses energy, resulting in a longer wavelength). Now, let's contrast this with how it interacts with matter. Matter, on the other hand, has a mass (or effectively, an "energy content", according to the equivalence principle), and light does not. Matter follows a specific path through spacetime, known as the geodesic, which is determined by the gravitational field. When an object with mass falls into a black hole, it is subject to extreme tidal forces and spaghettification. This process tears it apart, and the matter gets compressed into the singularity at the center of the black hole. Therefore, a black hole's effects on light and matter differ only in how they interact with the extreme gravity of the black hole. The light's path changes, but it "escapes." The matter, well, it’s consumed.

How is the speed of gravity determined? The speed of gravity is, rather obviously, determined by the speed of light. That is to say, the speed with which gravitational interactions propagate away from their source is the speed of light in vacuum, the maximum speed that anything can travel. Why is that? Well, gravity is mediated by the massless spin-2 particle, the graviton. The speed of a massless particle – and in the current prevailing theories, the graviton is believed to be massless – is *c*, the speed of light. Hence, gravity propagates at the speed of light. A more nuanced exploration enters the realm of general relativity, where gravity is conceptualized not as a direct "force" but as a manifestation of the curvature of spacetime caused by mass and energy. This curvature itself propagates at *c*. Any change in the gravitational field, originating, for example, from the movement of a celestial body like the Sun, has its effects rippling outward through spacetime, traveling at light speed. This elegant description, however, is more philosophically descriptive than it is predictive. There are only a few, rather indirect, ways to measure the speed of gravity. The first demonstration followed some years after Einstein published his theory (although he had already correctly predicted it originally). The most precise confirmation that the speed of gravity is the speed of light came from observations of gravitational waves. We are talking about the mergers of black holes and neutron stars, some of which were also accompanied by observable electromagnetic counterparts (i.e., an associated flash of light). The simultaneous detection of both gravitational waves and electromagnetic radiation gave us the most precise confirmation that gravity indeed travels at *c*. This is so because the travel time of light can be, and has been, measured directly, both on its own and compared to the travel time of electromagnetic radiation. This method hinges on the sensitivity of advanced detectors like LIGO and Virgo, which can discern the infinitesimal stretching and squeezing of space. If the speed of gravity deviated at all from the speed of light, it would be immediately apparent. The fact that the two were perfectly matched provided the cleanest verification. And let me add, the most dramatic.

How can virtual particles become real particles e.g. while Hawking radiation? That explanation of Hawking radiation — so central to the popular imagination — is really not so good. We are, once again, talking about virtual particles, and these are an unavoidable part of the story. In relativistic quantum field theory, the vacuum is not empty. In fact, due to quantum uncertainty, it is teeming with virtual particles. The best, most sensible way to think about them is to acknowledge them as mathematical tools. They are not “real” particles in the same sense as electrons or photons, but they are part of the math. The math, properly applied, gives us the correct answers that we observe in experiments, i.e., the radiation. But what exactly does “real” mean, anyway? In the context that questions like this are always posed, “real” means something that an observer can detect directly by way of their instruments. This is in contrast to the “virtual” particles that cannot be detected directly. A good analogy to virtual particles is the process of renormalizing an equation: You need to add terms that cancel infinities to get a sensible answer. These terms don’t have a physical meaning, but they are essential to get to a useful result. So, without the virtual particles, which are only of mathematical usefulness in the quantum realm, we can't get any useful conclusions. But Hawking radiation, the emission of particles from a black hole due to quantum effects, provides a more significant example of a situation where virtual particles can become real. One simple way the Hawking radiation can come about is when a virtual pair forms near the event horizon of a black hole. One particle may cross the event horizon, while the other escapes to infinity. The particle that escapes becomes “real” and observable, taking away energy from the black hole, hence its mass, which is the essence of the Hawking radiation effect: the black hole is losing mass and eventually would evaporate after a very long time. But the problem with this explanation is that it does not align well with the quantum field theory. Quantum field theory does not suggest this mechanism as a method to explain Hawking radiation. According to relativity, gravity slows time (time dilation) and causes length contraction? Does Dark Energy, which is accelerating the expansion of the Universe, speed time and cause lengthening is space? In a nutshell, does the observed accelerated expansion of the universe have an effect on spacetime that is the mirror image of the effect of gravity? The intuitive appeal is undeniable. The situation is not quite so simple, alas. The effect of acceleration can be described in the framework of general relativity, it's just that the effects of a cosmological constant (i.e., the Dark Energy that’s accelerating the expansion of the universe) play out differently than those of, say, the gravitational field of a spherical object. The effects of all forms of energy density on the fabric of spacetime are fundamentally the same, just the curvature of spacetime looks different if the the energy density is distributed differently. Technically, a cosmological constant, usually denoted by the Greek letter lambda (Λ), is a term in the Einstein field equations that describes the energy density of the vacuum. So, because it has a constant energy density, it is not a force in the usual sense of the word. Λ does not “cause” spacetime to expand or contract. The expansion of the universe is a consequence of the energy density, irrespective of whether that energy density is, say, the mass of the Earth, or the energy of the vacuum, etc. In other words, the presence of Dark Energy has about the same effect on the “speed” of time and the “length” of space as the presence of any other kind of energy. So no, in a way that is both simple and nuanced. Now, where it gets interesting is when we consider the effects of the cosmological constant on the overall geometry of the expanding universe. A non-zero Λ has a profound effect on the topology of spacetime, but that's a discussion for another time. As for your initial question, the answer is complicated, but ultimately no. How is mass not conserved when it's literally E^2-p^2, and both quantities are conserved? As I have already demonstrated, the equation m 2 = E 2 − p 2 does indeed describe the invariant rest mass of a particle. But it does not tell the whole story. Nor does it describe mass conservation in interactions. One can, for example, consider the decay of a neutron. The neutron possesses an invariant rest mass. Say it decays into a proton, an electron and an antineutrino. Total energy and momentum are conserved -- and of course, the total mass before and after is not. One single massive neutron is the precursor and the sum of the rest masses of the proton, the electron, and the antineutrino is the result. The end product adds up to a lower rest mass. Which is the source of energy of the constituents. This, in itself, should tell you, at least in principle, that rest mass is not an invariant quantity. Indeed, the value of the rest mass can vary quite a bit depending on the system. In the past I pointed out a closed box containing particles, and that the rest mass of the system remains constant, regardless of internal interactions. Let me offer another demonstration of the rather important point: namely, that the rest mass of a system is equivalent to its internal energy-content. Imagine a charged object, surrounded by electromagnetic radiation (photons): The rest mass of that object plus surrounding photons is higher than the rest mass would be of an uncharged one. In other words, photons can be thought of as bits of mass. The electromagnetic energy stored by the system can translate to mass. You can consider the same thing inside any confining environment where the charged object is: The effective mass of the charged object increases further. It does not matter what form that energy is in: kinetic energy, potential energy, even the rest masses of constituent bits. The rest mass of the overall system is the equivalent of the total internal energy of the box material and everything it encloses. All of these effects are consistent with special relativity, that is to say, nothing you should be particularly surprised about.

Is there empirical evidence against John Moffat's modified gravity (MOG), also known as Scalar-Tensor-Vector-Gravity (STVG)? Yes, there is. MOG/STVG makes specific predictions that have been tested against observational data, and in many cases, it has been found to be inconsistent. One of the most significant tests involves the cosmic microwave background (CMB). The CMB, as we understand, is a faint afterglow of the Big Bang, and its fluctuations provide a snapshot of the universe in its infancy. MOG, like any gravitational theory, makes predictions about the nature of these fluctuations. However, the predictions made by MOG do not align well with the patterns observed in the CMB. Specifically, some features that are prominent in the CMB data are not readily explained by MOG, and fitting the theory to match the data requires, in many cases, the introduction of additional parameters, which diminishes the theory's original appeal. Another area where MOG faces challenges is in the realm of galaxy clusters. These massive structures, held together by gravity, have been extensively studied, and observations of their dynamics and mass distribution provide crucial tests for gravitational theories. While MOG can in some cases reproduce the observed behavior of individual galaxies, it faces difficulties when applied to the complexities of galaxy clusters. The observed distribution of mass and the velocities of galaxies within clusters do not always align with the expectations of the theory. Furthermore, as with many modified gravity theories, MOG can be difficult to reconcile with the precise measurements of the solar system. The perihelion precession of Mercury, for example, is a classic test of general relativity, and any alternative theory must also explain this effect accurately. While some versions of MOG have been adjusted to fit this data, the adjustments often introduce new issues in other areas. Therefore, though MOG has had its proponents, the weight of current empirical evidence does not favor it as a viable alternative to general relativity.

Is it true that everything travels at a constant velocity in deep space, near the speed of light? No. The answer to this question is a qualified, “no”. Let’s start with the qualification. What do you mean by “everything”? Do you mean elementary particles such as electrons, muons, quarks, and photons? Or perhaps atoms, molecules, asteroids, planets, black holes? Each case is different. Let us assume, for the sake of argument, that the question refers to isolated, unaccelerated particles, far from any massive object that would warp spacetime, i.e., in deep space and away from anything that exerts a gravitational force. Then, in a relativistic sense, all the massless particles, i.e., photons, are indeed traveling at the vacuum speed of light, c. And massive particles will inevitably be traveling at some other speed, v, such that v < c. It must be said that it is hard to conceive such an object; it would be required to be both isolated, i.e., with no force acting upon it, and also not be accelerating, which means that it must maintain constant velocity, at least over the time scale under consideration. It might be instructive to review what this means, just for clarity. If a body has constant velocity, in other words is not accelerating (i.e., its velocity is constant), then it must have its (Newtonian) net force equal to zero. This is equivalent to saying that the total momentum is constant. Of course, this also assumes that the body is massive, if the speed is constant. If the body is massless, it still has to be traveling at constant velocity. However, there is a catch: The speed cannot be constant. This is a consequence of the fact that, according to the Special Theory of Relativity, the speed of light is constant in all inertial frames of reference. The speed must equal c and no value can be greater. So, in brief, we are talking about two cases. First, a massless particle such as a photon must travel at speed c. Second, a massive particle, such as an electron, can travel at any speed, v, where v < c. If the particle is traveling in deep space, there are no forces, i.e., no acceleration; therefore that speed is constant. The constant must, of course, be maintained in all the three spatial dimensions, i.e., x, y, and z, unless acted upon by an external force. So, is this correct? To be precise, yes. However, there is a further caveat, and that is acceleration. Let us imagine that one of the particles picks up some velocity, v, in some direction, say the x direction. Now imagine that a force acts upon the particle, i.e., an acceleration occurs. And assume that force acts in a direction perpendicular to the particle’s momentum. The speed is changed. This is correct.

How can Victor K. Toth say that matter does not create gravity, when the Nobel Prize winning physicist, Stephen Weinberg said that it’s a two-way street, “matter creates space-time, and space-time determines matter’s path”? Stephen Weinberg was, beyond any doubt, a giant of physics. However, a giant can occasionally be wrong, or at least imprecise. Weinberg was not describing the phenomenon of gravity; he was describing how general relativity, the theory that describes gravity, works. In general relativity, the presence of mass and energy warps spacetime; this distortion of spacetime then dictates how objects move. The popular description of gravity is that mass causes the force of gravity, and objects with mass are drawn together by it; that describes the effect, but not the cause. Technically, the cause is the warping of spacetime. But is that enough to say that the presence of mass and energy does *not* create gravity? Well, I would argue that there are two distinct concepts that need to be rigorously separated. On the one hand, there is General Relativity, which is a mathematical model, a set of equations. On the other hand, there is the universe itself, the reality that we perceive. In the formal language of general relativity, spacetime indeed warps in the presence of mass and energy, and this warping describes how objects move along what we call a “geodesic.” This is a completely self-consistent description, but it’s a mathematical one, not a description of physical reality. So to get back to the initial question, that's a simple yes. Matter, in a physical sense, does, in effect, “create” gravity. Without matter, there would be no spacetime, and there would be nothing to define the relative positions or accelerations of anything. However, in the mathematical model of general relativity, matter is *not* what “creates” gravity, spacetime curvature is. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

What is the cause of a black hole's immense strength? How is it possible for something to have infinite density and gravity? The short answer is, it doesn't. The singularity at the center is thought to have infinite density, yes, but as noted in many other answers, it's a mathematical point, not a physical object. And gravity, while undeniably intense near a black hole's event horizon, is not infinite. The misunderstanding stems from how we understand these objects. The “strength” of a black hole isn't inherent; it's purely a function of how much “stuff” formed the hole in the first place. More mass, more gravity. The gravitational force felt by a distant object is no different than if all that mass were packed into, say, a neutron star provided the mass is the same. It's really all about how far you are from the mass concentration within the black hole. The closer you get, the more intense the gravitational effects. The black hole's immense impact arises from its extreme compactness. Consider this: the Earth, if compressed into a ball the size of a marble, would become a black hole. The mass wouldn’t change, but its density would be astronomical, and the resulting gravity would be such that nothing, not even light, could escape its grasp. So, what's truly remarkable about a black hole is not its inherent strength or infinite properties. Instead, it’s the concentration of such a vast quantity of mass into an incredibly small space that allows for the extreme gravitational effects that make it, well, a black hole in the first place.

Why is graviton difficult to detect? Do we have any good reasons to believe it exits in the first place? That's a great question. When scientists finally can create a complete theory to describe the universe, gravitons may be needed to make the model complete. Do electromagnetic waves have momentum? If so, do waves and sound waves have momentum? Well, yes, electromagnetic waves do indeed have momentum. So, in a strict, fundamental sense, sound waves can be said to possess momentum, but in a way that’s vastly different from electromagnetic radiation. What has prevented Europe to stay unified like China since the collapse of Rome given they have far less people to govern than China? That's a fascinating question, and one that historians have debated for ages. It's tempting to look at China's enduring unity and contrast it with the fractured political landscape of Europe, especially after the fall of the Roman Empire. While population size undoubtedly played a role – China’s sheer demographic advantage offered a greater pool of resources and manpower for consolidation – it wasn’t the sole factor. Europe faced a complex interplay of forces that resisted unification.Firstly, consider the concept of *geography*. China enjoys natural barriers like the Himalayas and the Gobi Desert, which provided a degree of protection and facilitated the consolidation of power within more manageable geographical units. In contrast, Europe is far more fragmented: a series of peninsulas, islands, and navigable rivers that fostered trade and, paradoxically, also facilitated the rise of competing polities. The rugged terrain of the Alps served as a refuge for numerous isolated tribes.Secondly, one must factor in the *succession of empires* and the *political traditions* that developed in their wake. After Rome's fragmentation, Europe experienced a series of successor states, each with its own traditions, ambitions, and vested interests. This, coupled with the influence of the Holy Roman Empire, did not foster the kind of centralizing force witnessed in China.Thirdly, we have the *role of religion* and its influence. In China, Confucianism provided a unified moral and philosophical foundation for societal cohesion and bureaucratic centralization. In Europe, the Catholic Church, while acting as a unifying force to some extent, also introduced its own complexities, often leading to conflicts with secular powers while also, ironically, strengthening the importance of local authorities.Ultimately, many factors contributed to the disparate fates of the two regions. A unified China benefited from a relatively homogeneous culture, significant geographical barriers, and a strong emphasis on centralized governance that was passed down through the generations. Europe, on the other hand, was carved up into many separate nation-states that developed diverse languages, cultures, and political systems, all constantly vying for dominance.

Is there any way, other than throwing some mass in the opposite direction, to move forward in space? Well, that rather depends on what you mean by “move forward.” If you are referring to getting from point A to point B, then yes, obviously, as every spacecraft that ever existed illustrates. But let me clarify a couple of things first. The only way to change the speed of an object relative to an inertial frame of reference (i.e., to accelerate in any sense) is to change its momentum. And the only way to change its momentum is to apply a force, as any first-year physics student knows. Now, what does it mean to “apply a force?” Newton's Third Law states that for every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction. So, if you exert a force on X to push, well, you get pushed back. Consider the question of “throwing some mass in the opposite direction.” A rocket burns fuel and expels the exhaust gasses in the opposite direction; those gasses “push” against the rocket, which gives it the necessary forces to accelerate. That’s all good, but a rocket is not the only example of a vehicle that uses this trick. One can propel oneself forward in space in any number of ways, assuming one has a suitable medium to operate on. The force isn’t necessarily tied to mass. You can use the force of electricity or magnetism to accelerate. You can, in principle, use the repulsive force to propel you forward. This is how a solar sail works. Of course, all of these depend on something to shove against. The only other way to move forward is to warp spacetime itself. And that's the very stuff of science fiction. The Alcubierre drive, for instance, is a theoretical concept that involves creating a "bubble" of spacetime around a spacecraft and moving that bubble through space. A spacecraft inside a bubble would not experience acceleration, so there is no need to conserve momentum. As far as known physics is concerned, we don't have the technological ability to do any of this. But who knows, 100 or 200 years from now, the answer might be different.
