If a light ray of white light is bent by the gravity of a massive object like a star, does the light ray undergo diffraction and turn into a rainbow? No, it does not. And let me explain why. The phenomenon you are describing is usually associated with the deflection of light by a lens (or a prism). A lens focuses light, which effectively means that it spatially separates the different wavelengths. The shorter wavelengths (blue end of the spectrum) are bent more than the longer wavelengths (red). This separation is then easily detectable. The net result is that a typical lens, or a prism, can make a rainbow out of white light by its refractive action. However, when light passes by a massive object, it is bent by gravity, and there is no reason to think that different wavelengths of light are affected differently in this case. This is, to a good approximation, true. A massive object acts like a lens, but not in the same way a glass lens would. The bending is due to the curvature of spacetime and depends solely on how much the path of light is affected by it. It does not depend on the wavelength of the light. In fact, the bending of light by a gravitational field is best explained using general relativity, which predicts that all wavelengths, irrespective of their color, will bend by the same amount, assuming the same trajectory. The effect is purely geometric arising from the bending of spacetime itself. There is therefore no “rainbow effect” directly associated with the bending of light by a massive object. The light ray from the sun will change direction. But it will not break up into its constituent colors when deflected by the gravitational field of an object such as a star or a black hole.

Is Newton's conception of gravity as incompatible with Einstein's concept of gravity, as Einstein's is from the quantum? How, or how not? It may seem that way, but not really. Newton's theory of gravity certainly differs from Einstein's in some key aspects, but Einstein's theory, General Relativity, doesn't entirely invalidate Newton’s work. Instead, it expands upon it. Think of it this way: Newtonian gravity is a special case of General Relativity that is applicable when gravity is weak and speeds are much slower compared to the speed of light. So, for most everyday scenarios -- the apple falling from the tree, the moon orbiting the Earth, and even the motion of planets within our solar system -- Newton's laws are perfectly adequate. The mathematics is much simpler, too. However, when you deal with extremely massive objects, like black holes, or objects moving at speeds close to the speed of light, then it’s a different story. Newtonian gravity breaks down, and General Relativity becomes the necessary tool to describe the universe. Einstein's theory, you see, accounts for things that Newton's theory doesn't, such as the warping of spacetime by mass and the effects of gravity on light itself. Is General Relativity incompatible with quantum mechanics? Yes, in this case, there is an awkward tension. General Relativity describes gravity on a large scale, while quantum mechanics governs the subatomic world. The two theories are incredibly successful in their respective domains. However, despite numerous attempts over several decades, physicists have failed to reconcile them into a single, unified theory. A complete theory of quantum gravity, such as string theory or loop quantum gravity, is an active field of research, and the quest continues. The main problem is the extreme energies involved. For the effects of quantum gravity to be discernible, one needs to probe the spacetime structure at the smallest scales, which would require particle accelerators far more powerful than anything we can currently build. So, in short, while Newtonian gravity is a subset of General Relativity, the quantum picture of gravity eludes us still.

Can anything emerge in space other than mass and energy to be equivalent and convertible to mass or energy? If it can then how will we write E=mc2? Yes, it can. And it has to, if you want physics to make any sense at all. After all, without momentum, the entire concept of energy is rather meaningless. We typically do not write E = mc² because we are not in a framework where mass is the only thing. We need to use the full expression, which should include linear momentum. It then becomes a more versatile equation. The more complete version is E² = (pc)² + (mc²)², where p is the magnitude of the particle’s linear momentum, and m is the rest mass. These are, of course, the quantities that are conserved in reactions. The full equation still implies that, for a particle with rest mass m, energy and mass are equivalent. However, as I demonstrated in a recent post, this also means that the total mass of the *system* may be different from the sum of masses of the constituent bits. The rest mass of a system also includes their kinetic energy, but in all cases, the total rest mass of a closed system is always conserved. I will not go into detail on the derivation of the equation, as it is available in every textbook on the topic. However, the consequences are very important, because they explain a vast number of things if you accept the equation. This includes, but is not limited to, the fact that the speed of light is a universal constant, the equivalence of mass and energy, and time dilation. Also, just to be clear for the reader, the use of natural units (c = 1) simplifies the equations. It also makes it easier to appreciate the equivalence of units of energy, mass, and momentum.

Why does general relativity predict that the wavelength of light will be shifted due to the galaxies mass in an effect called gravitational redshift? General relativity predicts that light loses energy when escaping a gravitational field. This means that photons, as they climb out from under the gravitational pull of a massive object like a galaxy, get “tired.” Think of a ball thrown upwards, continually slowed down by the Earth's gravity. The ball loses kinetic energy, its speed decreases. Light, having no mass, cannot slow down. However, its energy is proportional to its frequency (and inversely proportional to its wavelength). Therefore, a photon losing energy means its frequency decreases, and its wavelength increases, or gets "redder," hence the term "redshift." This gravitational redshift effect isn't due to how the light *is* emitted, but to how it *travels* through the curved spacetime near a massive object that's distorting the fabric of space. It's a consequence of the equivalence principle, the notion that gravity and acceleration are indistinguishable. Imagine you're in an accelerating rocket, experiencing a constant "G-force." Light emitted from the floor of this rocket will appear to be shifted to lower frequencies as it travels upwards, similar to the effect of gravity on the surface of a massive object. This effect is most pronounced near extremely dense objects, such as neutron stars or, most dramatically, black holes. It is an unavoidable, yet subtle, consequence of the curvature of spacetime. What is the propagator for a massless scalar field, and how can you compute it using C++? I am often asked similar questions about the most esoteric of topics, and my answer, more often than I care to admit, is: I have no idea. However, I am familiar with the concept of a propagator. The propagator, in the context of quantum field theory, is a Green's function. Or rather, it *can* be a Green’s function. A Green’s function is, at its core, a solution to an inhomogeneous linear differential equation. Such equations are ubiquitous in theoretical physics. And as you may vaguely recall from your undergraduate classes, a Green’s function allows you to solve these types of differential equations. It tells you how a point-like source at a certain position affects the field. The propagator, in this context, is fundamentally about how a particle moves, and how it interacts. Now, the reason why it is helpful is that, armed with a propagator, you can, in principle, calculate all sorts of things. Given a theory and a Lagrangian, the propagator is the thing that you need to compute practically anything, such as scattering cross-sections, decay rates, and the like. Given that it's a “thing that you need,” it is something that you would like to know for the theory at hand. Now, you asked about the computation side of it. And you asked about C++. Well, C++ is just a tool though. There are countless things that you can do *with* it. Using C++ for this sort of computation, whether it's for a *massless* scalar field or anything else, comes down to understanding the underlying math and knowing how to translate that math into code. You would implement the relevant equations, perhaps using numerical techniques, depending on the complexity of the specific case. You would likely need to use libraries for numerical computation, such as Eigen or Armadillo, to handle the vector and matrix operations involved. You would need to know how to handle the limits, such as how to deal with infinities and singularities, which are a common issue when trying to construct a Green's function. So, what does the propagator look like for the massless scalar field? Well, it depends on the spacetime dimension and the gauge you choose. In four dimensions, using the Feynman propagator, it’s a rather simple expression in momentum space. In coordinate space, it gets a bit more complicated.

Does the existence of Hawking radiation suggest that nothing truly enters a black hole? The simple answer is no, but it is, of course, rather complicated. The popular explanation of what Hawking radiation "is" is often misunderstood. The most common narrative involving virtual particle pairs – one escaping, one falling in – is, in my humble opinion, a vast oversimplification, perhaps even misleading. If we adhere to Hawking's original findings, a more nuanced understanding emerges. The crux of the matter lies in the vacuum around a black hole, which isn't quite "empty." Instead, it undergoes gravitational vacuum polarization. This might sound esoteric, but it essentially implies that the quantum fields near a black hole behave differently, and these differences lead to, over immense timescales, the slow but inevitable emission of radiation. Now, the crucial point here is that the radiation isn't "from" anything inside the black hole; it's a product of the black hole's gravitational field interacting with the quantum vacuum. Think of it more as the black hole "boiling away" due to this quantum effect. This means, therefore, that the radiation is emitted *from* the vicinity of the black hole, not from within. Although the ultimate effect ends up being a gradual loss of mass, it doesn't necessarily mean that "nothing" enters as you suggest. But does anything *stay*? What would happen if something went through a black hole? That's a good question. Well, it depends. And the answer to this depends entirely on what “something" is. If “something” is a photon, then the answer is relatively simple. Relativity tells us that nothing, including photons, can escape a black hole once it has crossed the event horizon, which is the boundary beyond which escape from the black hole is impossible. So the photon simply joins the singularity, a point where all the mass of the black hole is concentrated, and likely gets converted into something we can’t even begin to imagine. However, if “something” is an object with mass, then things get a lot more complicated. The object will be subject to extreme tidal forces as it approaches the black hole. These forces arise because the gravitational pull of the black hole is much stronger on the side of the object closest to the black hole than on the opposite side. These tidal forces would stretch the object along the direction towards the black hole and compress it in the perpendicular direction. This process is often referred to as “spaghettification.” The point at which spaghettification becomes noticeable depends on the size of the black hole. For a supermassive black hole, such as the one at the center of our galaxy, the event horizon is so large that the object could, in principle, pass through the event horizon without experiencing the tidal forces. Even then, though, the result is far from pleasant. Whether or its spaghettified or not, everything that falls into a black hole ends up at the singularity, where the known laws of physics break down. So while no observable experiment can occur in such conditions (since an observer outside the black hole would not be able to watch), the object would inevitably be crushed to a point of infinite density. Furthermore, any information about that object, including its mass, charge, and angular momentum, would be lost to the outside world.
